title: Norris v. Independence County
description: Whether the Arkansas General Assembly has the authority to strip circuit courts of their constitutionally assigned original jurisdiction over facial constitutional challenges to state laws and confer that jurisdiction solely on the Arkansas Court of Appeals.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Bryan Norris, argued that Act 975 is unconstitutional because Amendment 80 of the Arkansas Constitution preserves the original jurisdiction of the circuit courts and confines the Court of Appeals to appellate jurisdiction only.
defendant_argument: The defendants, Independence County and the State of Arkansas, argued that Amendment 80, Section 10 grants the General Assembly the authority to establish court jurisdiction, and Section 9 allows them to amend the Supreme Court's rules to assign original jurisdiction for facial constitutional challenges to the Court of Appeals.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's dismissal, ruling that Act 975 of 2025 is unconstitutional because it attempts to alter the constitutionally fixed jurisdiction of the courts.

title: Gamble v. State
description: Whether Christopher Coy Gamble's custodial statement should be suppressed as the product of a pretextual arrest, and whether the precedent set by State v. Sullivan regarding pretextual arrests should be overruled.
plaintiff_argument: Gamble argued his custodial statement was obtained through an unlawful pretextual arrest and should be suppressed, and that the precedent of State v. Sullivan should not be overruled.
defendant_argument: The State argued Gamble's arrest was not pretextual, or if it was, the exclusionary rule did not apply, and in supplemental briefing, argued that State v. Sullivan should be overruled.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's denial of Gamble's motion to suppress and his motion to strike the venire, and overruled State v. Sullivan.

title: State v. Good Day Farm Arkansas
description: Whether the General Assembly has the authority to amend voter-initiated constitutional amendments and whether the germaneness requirement in Amendment 98 refers to 'section' or 'amendment'.
plaintiff_argument: The General Assembly lacks authority to amend voter-initiated constitutional amendments without popular approval, citing *Arkansas Game & Fish Commission v. Edgmon*, and that legislative amendments must be germane specifically to section 23 of Amendment 98, not the entire amendment.
defendant_argument: The General Assembly has constitutional authority under article 5, section 1, to amend voter-initiated laws with a two-thirds vote, and the word 'section' in Amendment 98's germaneness requirement was a drafting error and should be read as 'amendment'.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's ruling, holding that the General Assembly has the authority to amend voter-initiated laws and that the germaneness requirement refers to the entire amendment, not just a specific section.

title: Land v. BAS, LLC
description: Whether the Commissioner of State Lands provided constitutionally adequate notice to BAS before selling its Arkansas property to recover delinquent property taxes, with BAS arguing the notice was inadequate and the Commissioner arguing it was sufficient.
plaintiff_argument: BAS argued that the Commissioner violated its due process rights under federal and state constitutions by failing to provide proper notice of the tax sale, and that the sale constituted an unlawful taking, thus sovereign immunity should not apply.
defendant_argument: The Commissioner argued that the notice provided to BAS was constitutionally sufficient, and therefore, BAS's claims fail and are barred by sovereign immunity.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's denial of the Commissioner's motion for summary judgment, ruling that the Commissioner provided constitutionally sufficient notice and is entitled to sovereign immunity.

title: Spencer v. State
description: Whether a circuit court's gag order, restricting speech by trial participants and the public, violates constitutional rights to free speech and due process, or if it is a necessary measure to ensure a fair trial and protect the integrity of the case.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Aaron Spencer, argued that the gag order violated his due-process rights to a fair and public trial under the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments, as well as his First Amendment right to speak, constituting an unjustified prior restriction on content-based speech.
defendant_argument: The defendant, State of Arkansas, argued that the circuit court's gag order was within constitutional limits, protected the integrity of the case, and ensured a fair trial for both Spencer and the State amidst extensive pretrial publicity.
decision_outcome: The court granted the petition for writ of certiorari, issued the writ, and vacated the circuit court's gag order, finding it to be a plain, manifest, clear, and gross abuse of discretion.

title: McGill v. Thurston
description: Whether the popular name and ballot title for a proposed constitutional amendment concerning casino licenses in Pope County provide sufficient, non-misleading information to voters.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the popular name and ballot title are insufficient and misleading because they fail to disclose crucial information, imply prospective application when it is retroactive, incorrectly restrict future amendments, use inconsistent language regarding voter majority, and fail to disclose conflicts with federal law.
defendant_argument: The respondent and intervenors argued that the popular name and ballot title are sufficient, intelligible, honest, and impartial, as they adequately inform voters about the proposed amendment's scope, including the potential revocation of an existing license, and do not need to detail every possible future scenario or potential legal conflict.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petitioners' request to remove the measure from the ballot, finding the popular name and ballot title to be intelligible, honest, and impartial.

title: Paschall v. Thurston
description: Whether the popular name and ballot title for the proposed "Medical Marijuana Amendment of 2024" are sufficient and not misleading to voters.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners, Bill Paschall and Arkansans for Patient Access (APA), argued that the ballot title of the proposed constitutional amendment was sufficient and requested that votes for it be counted.
defendant_argument: The respondent, John Thurston (Secretary of State), initially argued that APA failed to meet the minimum-signature requirement, while the intervenors, Jim Bell and Protect Arkansas Kids (PAK), argued that the popular name and ballot title were misleading.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petitioners' request, denied the respondent's request, and granted the intervenors' request, enjoining the Secretary of State from canvassing or certifying ballots for the proposed amendment.

title: Thurston v. The League of Women Voters of Arkansas
description: Whether four Acts passed by the Arkansas General Assembly concerning election processes are constitutional under various provisions of the Arkansas Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the four Acts (736, 973, 249, and 728 of 2021) violated the Arkansas Constitution by burdening lawful, eligible voters' right to vote, making absentee voting harder, disenfranchising voters without photo ID, and impeding nonpartisan voter-support activities.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Acts were constitutional, enacted to protect the integrity of Arkansas elections and promote public confidence in election security, and that the circuit court erred by applying strict scrutiny as the right to vote in a particular manner is not a fundamental right.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's decision, holding that the four Acts are not clearly incompatible with the Arkansas Constitution and are therefore constitutional, dismissing the case.

title: Arkansas Department of Education v. Jackson
description: Whether the emergency clause of the LEARNS Act was procedurally valid, with the plaintiff arguing it was invalid due to a lack of a separate roll-call vote, and the defendant arguing it was valid as reflected in legislative journals.
plaintiff_argument: The LEARNS Act's emergency clause was invalid and ineffective because the General Assembly failed to pass it by a separate roll-call vote as required by the Arkansas Constitution.
defendant_argument: The LEARNS Act emergency clause received a separate roll-call vote, and the legislative journals, which are the official record, confirm its proper adoption.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's ruling, finding that the emergency clause of the LEARNS Act was validly enacted, and dismissed the case.

title: Eddie Armstrong & Lance Huey v. Thurston
description: Whether Arkansas Code Annotated section 7-9-111(i) unconstitutionally grants the State Board of Election Commissioners discretion to certify ballot titles, and whether the proposed ballot title for an amendment authorizing adult-use cannabis is legally sufficient.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the ballot title was sufficient and that Arkansas Code Annotated section 7-9-111(i) was unconstitutional because Article 5, Section 1 of the Arkansas Constitution mandates the Board to certify titles without discretion.
defendant_argument: The defendants and intervenors argued that section 7-9-111(i) was constitutional and that the ballot title was insufficient and misleading due to omissions regarding THC dosage limits, child protection, industrial hemp effects, facility details, and the definition of 'adult'.
decision_outcome: The court granted the petition, ruling that Arkansas Code Annotated section 7-9-111(i) is unconstitutional and that the proposed ballot title is sufficient, ordering the Secretary of State to certify it for the ballot.

title: Arkansas Department of Finance & Administration v. 2600 Holdings, LLC
description: Whether sovereign immunity bars 2600 Holdings' claims for a writ of mandamus and declaratory judgment against state agencies involved in medical marijuana licensing, and whether the circuit court has subject-matter jurisdiction over these claims.
plaintiff_argument: 2600 Holdings argued that sovereign immunity does not bar its request for a writ of mandamus, as provided by the Arkansas Constitution, and that its claim for declaratory relief should survive because the State's actions were illegal or unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The Arkansas Department of Finance and Administration, Arkansas Alcoholic Beverage Control Division, and Arkansas Medical Marijuana Commission argued that sovereign immunity bars both the writ of mandamus and declaratory judgment claims, and that the circuit court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction over the claims.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of the motion to dismiss regarding the writ of mandamus, but reversed the denial of the motion to dismiss for the declaratory relief claim, and dismissed claims seeking relief under the APA for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

title: Palade v. Board of Trustees of the University of Arkansas System
description: Whether the circuit court erred in dismissing the appellants' claims regarding the University of Arkansas System's revised faculty tenure policy on the grounds of lack of standing, unripeness, and nonjusticiability.
plaintiff_argument: The appellants, tenured faculty members, argued that the circuit court erred by dismissing their claims, asserting that the Revised Policy unilaterally and impermissibly modified their contractual and constitutional rights, and that their claims were justiciable and ripe for adjudication.
defendant_argument: The Board of Trustees argued that the appellants lacked standing, their claims were unripe and nonjusticiable, and that the Revised Policy merely clarified existing conduct standards without infringing on rights.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Arkansas affirmed the circuit court's dismissal of the appellants' claims, finding them nonjusticiable due to lack of standing and unripeness.

title: Rutledge v. Remmel
description: Whether Attorney General Leslie Rutledge is immune from lawsuits alleging she exceeded her authority and illegally exacted funds, with plaintiffs arguing she is not immune because her actions were ultra vires and malicious, and the Attorney General arguing she is protected by sovereign and statutory immunity.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General exceeded her authority by filing briefs in national litigation without state interest, spending public funds on consumer education for self-promotion, and engaging in partisan activities, thus she is not entitled to sovereign or statutory immunity. They sought an injunction and repayment of funds.
defendant_argument: Attorney General Leslie Rutledge argued she is protected by sovereign immunity for official capacity claims and statutory immunity for individual capacity claims, as her actions were within the scope of her employment and not malicious.
decision_outcome: The court reversed and dismissed the claim for injunctive relief and the illegal-exaction claim against the Attorney General in her individual capacity, while dismissing the appeal for the illegal-exaction claim against her in her official capacity, remanding it to the circuit court.

title: Bentonville School District v. Sitton
description: Whether the Bentonville School District's mask policy violated parents' constitutional rights and whether the District had the authority to implement such a policy.
plaintiff_argument: The District's mask policy violated parents' constitutional rights to care for their children and was enacted without proper authority.
defendant_argument: The District's mask policy was authorized to promote student health and safety and did not violate constitutional rights.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's temporary restraining order, finding that the parents failed to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits regarding their constitutional claims and the District's authority to implement the policy.

title: Arkansas Department of Health v. Solomon
description: Whether the circuit court had subject-matter jurisdiction and whether the State's refusal to renew a professional license without proper notice and hearing violated due process and equal protection, thereby being barred by sovereign immunity, and if a preliminary injunction was properly issued.
plaintiff_argument: Solomon argued that the Board's actions violated his due process and equal protection rights by not providing proper renewal notice or a hearing, and that the circuit court had jurisdiction.
defendant_argument: The State argued the circuit court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction, the lawsuit was barred by sovereign immunity, and the preliminary injunction was improperly granted.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part, reversed and dismissed in part, and reversed and remanded in part, upholding the circuit court's jurisdiction over constitutional claims and the denial of sovereign immunity for the due process claim, but dismissing the equal protection claim and remanding the preliminary injunction for further findings while keeping it in effect.

title: Edwards v. Thomas
description: Whether Arkansas Code Annotated section 27-34-106(a) violates the separation-of-powers doctrine, with the plaintiff arguing it is a constitutional substantive rule of law and the defendant arguing it is an unconstitutional procedural rule.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Arkansas Code Annotated section 27-34-106(a) is a substantive rule of law and therefore constitutional, precluding the defense from using failure to use a child safety seat as evidence of comparative fault.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that Arkansas Code Annotated section 27-34-106(a) is procedural law, unconstitutional, and thus the defense should be allowed to use failure to use a child safety seat as evidence of comparative fault.
decision_outcome: The court held that Arkansas Code Annotated section 27-34-106(a) is more substantive than procedural and does not violate the separation-of-powers doctrine, thereby answering the certified question in the negative.

title: McCarty v. Arkansas State Plant Board
description: Whether Arkansas Code Annotated § 2-16-206(a), which allows private entities to appoint members to the Arkansas State Plant Board, is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that Arkansas Code Annotated § 2-16-206(a) is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative appointment power to private entities.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that Arkansas Code Annotated § 2-16-206(a) is constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's finding, holding that Arkansas Code Annotated § 2-16-206(a) is unconstitutional and remanded with instructions to remove the unconstitutionally appointed Board members.

title: Thurston v. Safe Surgery Arkansas
description: Whether Arkansas Code Annotated section 7-9-601(b), which mandates that sponsors of initiative petitions obtain state and federal criminal background checks for paid canvassers from the Arkansas State Police and certify they passed, is unconstitutional because compliance is impossible, thereby infringing on the people's initiative and referenda rights.
plaintiff_argument: Safe Surgery Arkansas (SSA) argued that sections 7-9-601(b)(1) and (b)(3) are unconstitutional because it is impossible to obtain federal background checks from the Arkansas State Police (ASP) as required, making it impossible to certify that paid canvassers have passed such checks, thus violating Amendment 7's protection of initiative and referenda rights.
defendant_argument: Thurston argued that the circuit court lacked jurisdiction, that compliance with the statute was not impossible and could be achieved in various ways, and that the antifraud requirements served important state interests. Thurston also contended the preliminary injunction was overbroad.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's preliminary injunction, ruling that Arkansas Code Annotated section 7-9-601(b)(1) and (b)(3) are unconstitutional because it is impossible for initiative sponsors to comply with the federal background check requirements, and thus enjoined their enforcement.

title: Convent Corp. v. City of North Little Rock
description: Whether the City of North Little Rock's condemnation of Convent Corporation's property and its associated ordinances and procedures are constitutional and legally sound, particularly regarding due process, vagueness, and bills of attainder.
plaintiff_argument: Convent argued that the City's condemnation decision was not supported by substantial evidence, was arbitrary and capricious, violated due process (inadequate notice, meaningful hearing, opportunity to repair), its ordinances were unconstitutionally vague, and the resolution was an unlawful bill of attainder. Convent also contended that the circuit court erred by dismissing its constitutional, civil-rights, and trespass claims for failure to exhaust administrative remedies.
defendant_argument: The City argued that its condemnation decision was supported by substantial evidence, its procedures and ordinances were constitutional, Convent lacked standing, and Convent failed to exhaust administrative remedies for some claims. The City also asserted that Convent's vagueness claim was raised too late and the bill of attainder claim was invalid as the condemnation was an administrative, not legislative, act.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part (facial due-process claim, bill of attainder, vagueness, denial of motion to strike), reversed and remanded in part (dismissal of constitutional, civil-rights, and trespass claims for failure to exhaust administrative remedies, as-applied due-process claim), and dismissed as moot in part (administrative appeal of condemnation decision).
